sections.skill: Identify a real, frequent customer problem

questions.prompt: Which statement describes the strongest customer problem?

choices.text: Some people might enjoy a new kind of phone case someday.
Restaurant owners spend hours each week fixing their online menus.
My friends said a glow-in-the-dark mug sounds kind of fun.
Everyone would probably like more free time in their lives, so it is a problem.

questions.correct_answer: Restaurant owners spend hours each week fixing their online menus.
questions.intro: A good business idea starts with a real problem. A real problem happens often, matters to the person, and is something they already spend time or money trying to solve. "People might like this" is weak. "Parents in my neighborhood drive 30 minutes twice a week to a tutor" is strong, because it describes a costly habit that already exists. Look for complaints, workarounds (homemade fixes), and money already being spent.
questions.feedback: Hours spent every week on a task is a frequent, costly problem people already deal with.

questions.prompt: What is a "workaround"?

choices.text: A product that has already solved the problem fully for everyone
A complaint posted online about a company's prices
A business rule that customers must follow before buying
A homemade fix people use because no good solution exists yet

questions.correct_answer: A homemade fix people use because no good solution exists yet
questions.intro: A good business idea starts with a real problem. A real problem happens often, matters to the person, and is something they already spend time or money trying to solve. "People might like this" is weak. "Parents in my neighborhood drive 30 minutes twice a week to a tutor" is strong, because it describes a costly habit that already exists. Look for complaints, workarounds (homemade fixes), and money already being spent.
questions.feedback: Workarounds, like spreadsheets taped together, are clues that a real problem exists.

questions.prompt: Nina notices dog owners in her building tie their dogs outside the grocery store for 20 minutes. What does this suggest?

choices.text: Nothing useful, because the owners have not complained yet
Proof that a dog-sitting business will certainly succeed
A real, repeated problem that a service might solve
A sign that dog owners do not care about their pets at all

questions.correct_answer: A real, repeated problem that a service might solve

Look for complaints, workarounds (homemade fixes), and money already being spent.
questions.feedback: A repeated, inconvenient habit is a clue to a real problem worth testing.

questions.prompt: Which clue best shows people already spend money on a problem?

choices.text: A news story says homework levels have changed over time.
Local parents pay 40 dollars an hour for help with math homework.
Students post jokes online about long homework assignments.
Parents say math homework is "annoying" whenever they are asked about it.

questions.correct_answer: Local parents pay 40 dollars an hour for help with math homework.

Look for complaints, workarounds (homemade fixes), and money already being spent.
questions.feedback: Money already being spent is strong evidence a problem matters.

questions.prompt: Which is the best first question for finding a real problem?

choices.text: Would you buy my new homework app if I built it for you someday?
How much would you pay for anything I decide to sell?
What tasks take up your time each week that you dislike?
Do you agree my idea is clever and worth trying out?

questions.correct_answer: What tasks take up your time each week that you dislike?
questions.intro: A good business idea starts with a real problem. A real problem happens often, matters to the person, and is something they already spend time or money trying to solve. "People might like this" is weak. "Parents in my neighborhood drive 30 minutes twice a week to a tutor" is strong, because it describes a costly habit that already exists. Look for complaints, workarounds (homemade fixes), and money already being spent.
questions.feedback: Asking about real tasks and frustrations uncovers problems without pushing an idea.

questions.prompt: People wait 15 minutes in line for coffee each morning. Which part is the problem?

choices.text: The coffee shop's menu
The 15-minute wait
The price of coffee
An order-ahead app

questions.correct_answer: The 15-minute wait
questions.intro: Start with the problem, not your product. Think of a person stuck in a long line at a coffee shop every morning. The problem is wasted time. A product, like an order-ahead app, is one possible answer. If you start with "I want to build an app," you may build something nobody needs. If you start with "people wait 15 minutes every morning," you can test different answers and keep the one people choose. Problems come first; products come second.
questions.feedback: The wasted time is the problem.

questions.prompt: Which statement starts with a problem?

choices.text: I will sell bright blue backpacks to everyone.
Many renters struggle to find quiet study spaces nearby.
My brand will have a lightning bolt logo.
I want to build an app with many cool features for people.

questions.correct_answer: Many renters struggle to find quiet study spaces nearby.
questions.intro: Start with the problem, not your product. Think of a person stuck in a long line at a coffee shop every morning. The problem is wasted time. If you start with "people wait 15 minutes every morning," you can test different answers and keep the one people choose. Problems come first; products come second.
questions.feedback: It names a struggle people have.

questions.prompt: Why start with the problem?

choices.text: So the product is as expensive as possible
So you can skip talking to customers completely
So you do not build something nobody needs
So you can choose a business name sooner

questions.correct_answer: So you do not build something nobody needs

questions.feedback: Understanding the problem first keeps you from building the wrong thing.

choices.text: Making the coffee cups larger than before
Adding a second cashier during rush hour

Changing the color of the store sign

questions.correct_answer: Adding a second cashier during rush hour

questions.prompt: Which is a product, not a problem?

choices.text: Workers with no time to cook dinner
Families wasting food every week
A meal-planning app
Shoppers forgetting items at the store

questions.correct_answer: A meal-planning app

sections.relationship: A learner who misses MAIN may describe products instead of problems; one everyday example separates them.

sections.skill: Apply it: choose the problem worth testing

choices.text: Problem 3, because parking is a common topic that comes up in towns
Problem 1, because people already pay to solve it every week
None, because none of these is a real problem at all
Problem 2, because more colors would be fun to design

questions.correct_answer: Problem 1, because people already pay to solve it every week
